---
name: datum-3round-adversarial-review
description: "3-round adversarial review pattern for datum — domain audits and TDD commit reviews; filed as datum#134"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  scope: project
  expires_after_days: 180
  last_verified: 2026-06-12
  originSessionId: 2c5a3bd7-ae53-4761-b3a1-925307f8928a
---

3-round adversarial review pipeline for datum's review phase. Validated on epic-30 domain contract audit (2026-06-12). Filed as feature request at gitrdunhq/datum#134.

**Round 1**: One Opus agent per domain/layer — in-shape, out-shape, internal consistency, correctness.

**Round 2**: One Opus agent per concern dimension across all layers — data flow, error propagation, layer violations, concurrency, cross-platform divergence, silent failures.

**Round 3 (mega adversarial)**: 3 Opus agents receive all Round 1+2 findings and are explicitly told to DISPROVE them, find missed issues, and identify systemic root causes. Framing as "disprove" (not "confirm") is critical to quality.

**Synthesizer**: One Opus agent → structured JSON → Python → prioritized remediation plan (P0-P3, effort, fix dependency graph).

**Why:** Filed as datum skill (not WFC) because it belongs in the datum review phase. Applies to both domain architecture reviews AND TDD commit reviews before merge gate.

Related: [[datum-epic-30-thunderdome]]

# Domain Audit: Record-ML (MLInfrastructure)

---

## 3. Internal Consistency Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| IC-1 | LOW | `cleanedMicAudioPath` in DuckDB schema (`recordings.cleaned_mic_audio_url`) aligns with RF Domain but not CPF — cross-platform portability gap |
| IC-2 | MEDIUM | `context_cache` table has no PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint — concurrent puts for same `(query_text, provider_id)` can create duplicate rows |
| IC-3 | MEDIUM | `DuckDBCommitmentStore` opens its own `Database` handle against the same file as `DuckDBReaderActor` — two separate Database handles on same file, latent write conflict risk |
| IC-4 | MEDIUM | `MCPSummarizationPlugin` hardcodes `"id": 1` in JSON-RPC requests but does not validate response `id` matches — no response correlation enforcement |

## 4. Correctness Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| C-1 | MEDIUM | `getSegments` in `DuckDBReaderActor+Diarization.swift:29` uses `try?` on word timing decode with NO log — truly silent; corrupt `word_timings` JSON returns `wordTimings: nil` with zero diagnostic signal |
| C-2 | MEDIUM | `getWordTimings` in `DuckDBReaderActor+Transcript.swift:35` uses `try?` with a warning log — partially mitigated, caller cannot distinguish "no timings" from "corrupt timings" |
| C-3 | **HIGH** | `saveSummary` fallback `?? "{}"` in `DuckDBWriterActor+Summary.swift:10` — on `String(data:encoding:)` returning nil, stores empty JSON object; subsequent `getSummary` call fails with `readFailed` while the underlying encode error is masked |
| C-4 | MEDIUM | `deleteRecording` wraps `recordingNotFound` as `deleteFailed(underlying: recordingNotFound)` — double-wrapping loses specificity |
| C-5 | LOW | `DuckDBReaderActor.init` uses `print()` for fatal init error instead of logger — unstructured output |
| C-6 | LOW | `DuckDBCommandServer` has overlapping DDL validation in both `validate()` and `adminExecute` — combined effect is correct but maintenance-confusing |
| C-7 | CLEAN | ROLLBACK path logged at `.error` with underlying error — correct after epic-30 fix |
| C-8 | CLEAN | JSON parse errors in `MCPSummarizationPlugin` logged with specific failure reason — correct after epic-30 fix |
| C-9 | CLEAN | Missing prompt templates throw `SummarizationError.missingTemplate` — correct after epic-30 fix |
| C-10 | CLEAN | CalendarError maps to `.accessDenied` vs `.systemError` specifically — correct after epic-30 fix |

## 5. Summary

Record-ML layer is solid. All domain protocols correctly implemented, schema consistent with domain types, error handling generally strong. **Top priority:** `saveSummary` `?? "{}"` fallback (C-3) — stores garbage JSON on encode failure, causing confusing `readFailed` on next load. Second: `context_cache` missing UNIQUE constraint (IC-2) — duplicate cache rows possible under concurrent puts. Third: `getSegments` truly-silent word timing decode failure (C-1) — add warning log to match `getWordTimings` pattern.

# Domain Audit: Record-Presentation

---

## 3. Internal Consistency Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| IC-1 | CLEAN | All 15 ViewModels are `@Observable @MainActor` — consistent |
| IC-2 | MEDIUM | `SearchViewModel.searchError: UserFacingError?` never rendered in any View — search failures are typed at ViewModel but silently swallowed from user perspective |
| IC-3 | LOW | Most error state is `String?` not typed — `MenuBarViewModel.errorMessage`, `MeetingLibraryViewModel.errorMessage`, etc. Acceptable for v1 but limits testability |
| IC-4 | MEDIUM | `ModelDownloadViewModel` does direct `UserDefaults.standard` reads/writes and `FileManager` calls — minor layer leak, should be behind protocol seams for testability |
| IC-5 | LOW | `MeetingDetailViewModel.notesError` and `.saveError` are typed `any Error` but never rendered in any View |
| IC-6 | MEDIUM | `MenuBarViewModel.errorMessage` not cleared in `stopRecordingTapped()` — stale error from a prior start failure persists through a successful stop+transcribe cycle |

## 4. Correctness Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| C-1 | MEDIUM | `BroadsheetAppStateLifecycle.selectMeeting()` lines 18-19 — `loadDetail` errors logged but not surfaced; failed meeting load silently shows stale content |
| C-2 | LOW | `SettingsViewModel.errorMessage` not cleared on success for `loadProfiles()`, `deleteProfile()`, `saveAudioDeviceSelection()` — stale error persists until new failure |
| C-3 | CLEAN | All async Task captures use `[weak self]` — no retain cycles found across 15 ViewModels |
| C-4 | LOW | `MeetingLibraryViewModel.groupByDay()` lines 76-77: `groups[$0]!` force unwrap — safe (key guaranteed inserted in same loop) but should use `groups[$0, default: []]` |
| C-5 | LOW | `MenuBarViewModelStorage.deleteRecording()` and `exportRecording()` don't clear `errorMessage` before new attempt — stale error from prior op can confuse |

## 5. Summary

Presentation layer contract is solid. All ViewModels correctly `@Observable @MainActor`, every async Task captures `[weak self]`, zero Infrastructure imports. **Top priority:** `SearchViewModel.searchError` is set but never rendered in any View — search failures are invisible to users. Second: `MenuBarViewModel.errorMessage` not cleared on `stopRecordingTapped()` — stale error banner after successful recording. Third: `ModelDownloadViewModel` direct `UserDefaults`/`FileManager` access — minor layer violation reducing testability.

# Domain Audit: Record-App/Sources/Business

---

## 3. Internal Consistency Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| IC-1 | CLEAN | All 22 Business files import only `Foundation`, `Logging`, and `Domain` — no infrastructure imports |
| IC-2 | MEDIUM | `QueryContextUseCase` constructed with `mcpConsentGranted = false` in `AppAssemblerBuilders.buildEngine()` (line 129) — MCP context pipeline silently disabled regardless of user's config setting |
| IC-3 | MEDIUM | `PipelineCoordinator` exposes sub-use-cases as `public let` — callers can bypass coordinator's state machine and generation guard; TODO exists but unresolved |
| IC-4 | LOW | `StopAndTranscribeUseCase` and `ExportAudioUseCase` use `FileManager` / `FileHandle` directly — technically Foundation, not Infrastructure, but leaks filesystem concerns into Business layer |
| IC-5 | LOW | Sub-assemblers (`AudioSubAssembler.build()`, `TranscriptionSubAssembler.build()`) take concrete `DuckDBReaderActor` / `DuckDBWriterActor` in their signatures — not testable with mock storage without subclassing |
| IC-6 | LOW | `InMemoryCommitmentStore` fallback in AppAssembler if DuckDB commitment store init fails — commitment data silently in-memory (lost on restart), error is logged but not propagated |

## 4. Correctness Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| C-1 | MEDIUM | `SummarizeMeetingUseCase.summarize()` silently swallows summary persistence failures (lines 98-108) — caller never knows persistence failed, user sees summary in-session but it's missing on app relaunch |
| C-2 | CLEAN | WAV preservation guaranteed on persistence failure — explicit check at `StopAndTranscribeUseCase` lines 76-91; WAV deleted only on `CancellationError` before persistence |
| C-3 | CLEAN | All 22 use cases maintain strict import discipline |
| C-4 | MEDIUM | INV-001 invariant (`AudioFile.id == RecordingSession.id`) documented in code but not runtime-asserted — if storage assigns its own ID, transcript update would target wrong recording |

## 5. Summary

Business layer contract is solid. Strict import discipline (Foundation + Logging + Domain only), clean actor-based concurrency, thorough cancellation paths. **Top priority:** `mcpConsentGranted = false` hardcoded in `buildEngine()` silently disables MCP context for all users if it's meant to be production-enabled. Second: `SummarizeMeetingUseCase` swallowing persistence failures — user sees summary in-session then loses it. Third: expose `PipelineCoordinator` sub-use-cases via coordinator only (enforce state machine).

# Domain Audit: Record-Audio (AudioInfrastructure)

---

## 3. Internal Consistency Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| IC-1 | LOW | AEC far-end buffer reuse: every 256-sample mic chunk in a single `process()` call shares the same 256-sample far-end reference — degrades echo cancellation on longer mic buffers |
| IC-2 | MEDIUM | `errorHandler` not wired in `CoreAudioTapCaptureActor` or `WAVCleanedAudioSink` — write failures increment counter but are never surfaced to Business layer |
| IC-3 | LOW | `CameraDetector` protocol defined locally in `CameraSessionDetector.swift`, not in Domain — layer violation |
| IC-4 | LOW | `ConverterErrorTracker` (`CoreAudioTapCaptureActorSupport.swift:230`) is `@unchecked Sendable` with no synchronization — safe in practice (single tap queue) but implicit |

## 4. Correctness Findings

| ID | Severity | Description |
|---|---|---|
| C-1 | MEDIUM | Write failures silently swallowed — `errorHandler` is `nil` on both WAVWriter instances; disk-full produces truncated recordings with no user notification |
| C-2 | LOW | `MicTapBridge.swift:47` force unwrap on `AVAudioPCMBuffer` init — justified (known-good Float32 format) but defensive `guard let` preferred |
| C-3 | LOW | Dead code in `CoreAudioTapCaptureActorHAL.swift` — `createProcessTap()` duplicates logic already inlined in `start()` but is never called |
| C-4 | LOW | `AudioSessionListenerBox.registeredDevices` has mixed synchronization: `NSLock` in `removeAllListeners()`, actor isolation in `startListening()` — safe due to deinit ordering but fragile pattern |
| C-5 | LOW | `WaveformProcessor.swift:69` force unwrap `fftSetupCache.keys.first!` — justified by `count >= 16` guard |

## 5. Summary

Audio pipeline contract is solid. All 11 Domain protocols implemented correctly, Float32/Int16 boundaries consistent, RecordingID threaded faithfully, teardown deterministic. **Top priority:** Wire `errorHandler` in both `CoreAudioTapCaptureActor` and `WAVCleanedAudioSink` (IC-2/C-1) — without it, disk-full scenarios produce truncated recordings with no user notification. Secondary: fix AEC far-end buffer reuse (IC-1) for longer mic buffers. Dead code in `CoreAudioTapCaptureActorHAL.swift` should be removed.

# Dream: Memory Consolidation

Perform a reflective memory consolidation pass. When this skill is invoked, Claude executes it directly — no sub-agent needed.

## Step 1: Resolve environment

Compute the paths you'll be working with:

**Project hash**: Current working directory with every `/` replaced by `-`.
- CWD `/Volumes/Extra/repos/personal/bodyMan` → hash `-Volumes-Extra-repos-personal-bodyMan`

**Memory directory**: `~/.claude/projects/{hash}/memory/`

**Global memory directory**: `~/.claude/memory/global/`

**Transcripts directory**: `~/.claude/projects/{hash}/`
- The `.jsonl` files here are conversation transcripts (one per session)

**Index file**: `{memory_dir}/MEMORY.md`

**Global index**: `~/.claude/memory/global/MEMORY.md`

**Episodic directory**: `{memory_dir}/episodic/`

**Project CLAUDE.md**: `{cwd}/CLAUDE.md` (may or may not exist)

**Today's date**: use the current date in YYYY-MM-DD format

> If the memory directory doesn't exist, tell the user there's nothing to consolidate yet and stop.

> If the user provided explicit paths (e.g., in a test context or as arguments), use those instead of auto-detecting.

---

## Phase 0 — Staleness Audit

Before orienting on content, flag stale memories so they don't mislead the consolidation.

Run the audit script:
```
uv run ~/.wfc/skills/wfc-closeout/scripts/memory_audit.py {memory_dir}
```

If the output is a non-empty JSON array, surface the flagged memories to the user:

> These memories may be stale and need verification before you continue:
> - `{name}` ({type}, {age_days} days old) → recommended action: **{action}**
>
> For each: verify it's still accurate, update it, or I'll archive it. Type "skip" to proceed without action.

**Action meanings:**
- `verify` — expired but recent enough that you should confirm it's still accurate
- `archive` — significantly past expiry; move to `{memory_dir}/archive/` rather than delete

Wait for user response before proceeding to Phase 1 (unless the array is empty, in which case proceed immediately).

---

## Phase 1 — Orient

1. List the memory directory to see what topic files already exist
2. Read `MEMORY.md` to understand the current sectioned index (Daily drivers / Project state / Patterns & pitfalls / References)
3. Skim 3–4 of the existing topic files to understand their structure — prevents near-duplicate creation

---

## Phase 2 — Gather recent signal

Look for new information worth persisting.

### 2a: Auto-extraction from transcripts

Find the 2 newest session transcript files:
```
ls -t {transcripts_dir}/*.jsonl | head -2
```

Run the extractor on them:
```
uv run ~/.wfc/skills/wfc-closeout/scripts/memory_extract.py {transcript1} {transcript2}
```

The output has three buckets: `high_confidence`, `medium_confidence`, `low_confidence`.

**High-confidence candidates** (explicit "remember X" / "always do Y" / "never do Z"):
- Auto-write these as memories without asking — they are explicit instructions.
- Write them to the correct section in MEMORY.md based on type.

**Medium-confidence candidates** (corrections, "we should", "actually"):
- Present them to the user in a compact list:
  > Found these potential memories from recent sessions — confirm, skip, or edit each:
  > 1. [suggested_type] "{source_quote}" → save as: `{suggested_name}`?
- Write the ones the user confirms.

**Low-confidence candidates**: skip unless user asks to review them.

### 2b: Manual signal from transcripts

Read the first 50–100 lines of the newest 1–2 transcript files to understand what sessions covered. Then grep narrowly for topics that seem worth persisting:
```
grep -n "term" {transcripts_dir}/{uuid}.jsonl | tail -30
```

> Never read an entire JSONL file. Grep narrowly for things you already suspect matter. These files can be hundreds of megabytes.

### 2c: Drifted memories

Any existing memory file that contradicts what you now see in the codebase or transcripts should be corrected at the source.

### 2d: Episodic detection

Look in transcripts for the pattern: tried X → error/failure → switched to Y. These are candidates for episodic memories in `{memory_dir}/episodic/`.

Signals to grep for: "didn't work", "failed", "wrong", "switched to", "instead I", "turned out".

If you find a clear failure+pivot pattern, write it as an episodic memory (see Episodic Memory section below).

---

## Phase 3 — Consolidate

For each thing worth persisting, write or update a memory file.

### Scope assignment

Before writing, decide scope:
- **Global** (`~/.claude/memory/global/`): Swift language patterns, WFC workflow patterns, general engineering rules that apply across all projects
- **Project** (`{memory_dir}/`): decisions, constraints, deadlines, file paths, epic-specific context

Add `scope: global` or `scope: project` to the `metadata:` block.

### Frontmatter format

```markdown
---
name: short-kebab-case-slug
description: one-line summary — used to decide relevance in future sessions
metadata:
  type: user | feedback | project | reference | episodic
  scope: global | project
  expires_after_days: 60   # project/reference only; omit for feedback/user
  last_verified: YYYY-MM-DD
---

Memory content here.
```

For `feedback` and `project` types, include:
- **Why:** the reason this matters
- **How to apply:** when/where this guidance kicks in

**Merge, don't duplicate**: check existing topic files before creating a new one — similar content should be merged in.

**Absolute dates only**: convert relative dates to absolute dates using today as the anchor.

**Delete, don't annotate**: if an existing memory is wrong, fix or remove it.

**Link related memories**: use `[[slug]]` to reference related topic files.

**What NOT to save**: code patterns, file paths, git history, current task state, or anything already captured in CLAUDE.md.

### Section assignment for MEMORY.md

When writing to project or global MEMORY.md, insert the new pointer into the correct section (not the bottom):

| Type | Section |
|------|---------|
| `feedback` with "always"/"never"/"mandatory" in description | `## Daily drivers` |
| `project` | `## Project state` |
| `feedback` (nuanced, not daily) | `## Patterns & pitfalls` |
| `reference` | `## References` |

Never append to the bottom of an unstructured index. The sections must be preserved.

---

## Episodic Memory

Episodic memories capture specific events: what was tried, why it failed or worked, what the fix was.

Write them to `{memory_dir}/episodic/` (not the main memory dir).

```markdown
---
name: short-slug-epic-N
description: what was tried and what happened
metadata:
  type: episodic
  date: YYYY-MM-DD
  epic: "5.13"
  outcome: success | failure | partial
---
Body: what was tried, the error or failure, what the fix or pivot was.
```

After writing an episodic memory, add a pointer to `{memory_dir}/episodic/INDEX.md`.

---

## Phase 4 — Prune and index

Update `MEMORY.md` to stay **under 200 lines**. It's an index, not a dump.

Each entry is one line:
```
- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook under ~150 chars
```

**Prune**:
- Remove pointers to memories that are stale, superseded, or wrong
- Memories migrated to global scope: remove from project index (global MEMORY.md is loaded separately)
- If an index line is over ~200 characters, shorten it — move the detail to the topic file

**Add**: pointers to newly written or updated topic files, in the correct section

**Resolve**: if two entries contradict each other, fix the wrong one

**Section headers** must be preserved:
```
## Daily drivers (fires every session)
## Project state (time-sensitive)
## Patterns & pitfalls (timeless)
## References (where things live)
```

---

## CLAUDE.md reconciliation

If `{cwd}/CLAUDE.md` exists, review it briefly:
- If a convention in CLAUDE.md conflicts with a stored memory, the memory is wrong — fix it
- CLAUDE.md is authoritative for project conventions

---

## Wrap-up

Report back to the user:
- What was audited and verified/archived (if any)
- What auto-extracted memories were written
- What user-confirmed candidates were written
- What episodic memories were recorded
- What was pruned from the index
- Any CLAUDE.md conflicts that need user attention
- If nothing changed, say so explicitly — don't invent work

## Cross-Platform Divergence (Verified from Source Code)

### 1. Feature.swift -- CRITICAL (Codable roundtrip fatal crash)

**RF:** 17 cases (oss: 7, standard: 3, pro: 6, team: 4)
**CPF:** 24 cases (oss: 10 [+dictation, glossaryTech, glossaryPolitics, glossaryGeneral], standard: 3, pro: 6, team: 4, addon: 3 [vocabularyMedical, vocabularyLegal, vocabularyFinance])

**What breaks:** `Feature` is `String`-rawValue `Codable`. When CPF encodes `.vocabularyMedical` ("vocabularyMedical") and RF decodes it, `JSONDecoder` throws `DecodingError.dataCorrupted` because no matching case exists. The reverse direction has the same problem for `.dictation`, `.glossaryTech`, `.glossaryPolitics`, `.glossaryGeneral`. There is no `init(from:)` override with unknown-case handling -- the synthesized `Codable` crashes.

**Severity:** CRITICAL. Any config, license check, or feature-gate payload serialized on one target and deserialized on the other produces a fatal decode error.

**Files:**
- `/Volumes/Extra/repos/gitrdunhq/the-record-suite/Record-Foundation/Sources/Domain/Licensing/Feature.swift`
- `/Volumes/Extra/repos/gitrdunhq/the-record-suite/Record-CrossPlatform-Foundation/Sources/Domain/Licensing/Feature.swift`

### 2. LicenseTier.swift -- CRITICAL (Codable crash + security bypass)

**RF:** 4 cases (oss=0, standard=1, pro=2, team=3)
**CPF:** 5 cases (adds `addon` with rank=-1)

**Two bugs:**
1. **Codable crash:** CPF encodes `.addon` ("addon") -- RF decodes it and throws `DecodingError.dataCorrupted` (no `.addon` case).
2. **Security bypass:** `LicenseTier` is `Comparable` via `rank`. `.addon` has rank -1. Since `Feature.requiredTier` returns `.addon` for vocabulary features and the gating check is `currentTier >= feature.requiredTier`, ANY tier (including `.oss` at rank 0) satisfies `0 >= -1`. Vocabulary features are completely ungated on CPF targets.

**Severity:** CRITICAL. The rank-(-1) bug means paid add-on features require zero entitlement.

**Files:**
- `/Volumes/Extra/repos/gitrdunhq/the-record-suite/Record-Foundation/Sources/Domain/Licensing/LicenseTier.swift`
- `/Volumes/Extra/repos/gitrdunhq/the-record-suite/Record-CrossPlatform-Foundation/Sources/Domain/Licensing/LicenseTier.swift`

**RF:** 13 fields including `cleanedMicAudioPath: URL?` (added epic-28). Has a separate `RecordingMetadata+Codable.swift` extension with custom `init(from:)` that handles `cleanedMicAudioPath` via `decodeIfPresent`.

**CPF:** 24 cases (+dictation, glossaryTech, glossaryPolitics, glossaryGeneral, vocabularyMedical, vocabularyLegal, vocabularyFinance)

**RF:** 4 cases (oss=0, standard=1, pro=2, team=3)  
**CPF:** 5 cases (adds `addon` with rank=-1)

**Two bugs:**
1. **Codable crash:** CPF encodes `.addon` ("addon") — RF decodes it and throws `DecodingError.dataCorrupted` (no `.addon` case).

# Round 2: Layer Violations + Concurrency Cross-Dimensional Review

---

## Layer Violation Findings

### LV-1 — MEDIUM: Presentation imports 13+ concrete Business types

`Record-Presentation` imports concrete Business-layer types directly rather than through protocol abstractions. Presentation should depend only on protocols defined in Domain, not on concrete Business implementations.

**Impact:** Breaks testability — ViewModels cannot be unit-tested without instantiating real Business use cases.

---

## Concurrency Findings

### CC-1 — HIGH: `ConverterErrorTracker` unprotected mutable counter

`ConverterErrorTracker` in `CoreAudioTapCaptureActorSupport.swift` is `@unchecked Sendable` with a mutable counter that has no synchronization mechanism. In practice it runs on the tap queue (single-writer), but the lack of explicit synchronization is an implicit constraint that future refactors could easily violate.

**File:** `Record-Audio/Sources/AudioInfrastructure/CoreAudioTapCaptureActorSupport.swift:230`

---

### CC-8 — MEDIUM: `nonisolated(unsafe)` on `EKEventStore`

`EventKitPlugin.swift` uses `nonisolated(unsafe)` on an `EKEventStore` property to suppress concurrency warnings. `EKEventStore` is not thread-safe; this suppression hides a real concurrency hazard.

**File:** `Record-ML/Sources/MLInfrastructure/Calendar/EventKitPlugin.swift`

---

### CC-9 — MEDIUM: `nonisolated(unsafe)` on `DiarizerManager`

Similar pattern to CC-8 — `nonisolated(unsafe)` used to silence Swift concurrency on a class that is not designed for concurrent access.

---

## Summary

Top finding is CC-1 (ConverterErrorTracker mutable state) — high risk if the single-queue assumption is ever violated. LV-1 (Presentation concrete imports) is a testability debt item, not a runtime risk. CC-8/CC-9 (`nonisolated(unsafe)` usages) paper over real concurrency hazards that should be addressed with proper actor isolation or explicit locking.

input.prompt:
You are a research agent. Your job is to produce a dense, structured knowledge dump of git workflow best practices and variations — specifically to feed an architect who will design the best git workflow for a tool called "datum".

## datum context

datum is a multi-phase AI-assisted software engineering pipeline. Its git workflow has these constraints/characteristics:
- **Epic branches**: `datum/epic-NN-description` off main
- **TDD red→green→refactor phases**: each phase produces a commit; RED must be a failing test, GREEN is the fix, REFACTOR cleans up. These are intra-branch commits.
- **Parallel act agents**: multiple Claude Code sub-agents work on different TDD lanes simultaneously on the same branch. This causes file-lock collisions (datum#129 — agents using `git checkout` wipe each other's working-tree changes).
- **Squash before first push**: all local commits squash into one before the branch is published.
- **Hard gates**: plan_human_approval, triage_human_approval, merge_human_approval halt the pipeline until a human confirms.
- **Ratchet enforcement**: test count must never go below a floor (currently 829). The gate is checked before merge.
- **Act phase can have 5-15 TDD tasks running in parallel** across units A→F, some serial (A→B→C audio path) and some truly parallel (D/E/F).
- **Problem to solve**: parallel agents on one branch collide. We need an architecture where parallel TDD agents can work without stomping each other, then merge cleanly to the epic branch.

## What to research

Produce findings across these dimensions:

### 1. Branch strategies for parallel work
- Git worktrees (one worktree per parallel agent, merge to epic branch after)
- Feature sub-branches (one branch per TDD task, PR to epic branch)
- Stacked PRs / stacked diffs (Graphite, ghstack, git-branchless)
- Trunk-based with short-lived branches
- What big monorepo shops do (Google, Meta, Stripe)

### 2. Merge strategies
- Squash merge: pros/cons for aggregating multi-commit TDD work
- Rebase merge: preserves RED/GREEN/REFACTOR granularity, rebases onto epic branch
- Merge commit: creates explicit topology showing when parallel lanes merged
- Octopus merge: can merge 3+ branches simultaneously (risky but fast)
- Fast-forward only: strictest, requires linear history

### 3. Conflict resolution patterns for parallel agents
- Worktree isolation (each agent gets own worktree, no shared working tree)
- File-lock protocol (claim files before editing — git-based or external)
- Actor model for git ops (one git-ops coordinator, agents submit diffs)
- Patch-queue model (agents produce patches, coordinator applies serially)
- Pre-merge CI gate per agent lane

### 4. Commit discipline for TDD pipelines
- Conventional commits (feat/fix/test/refactor prefixes)
- Atomic commits (one logical change per commit — maps well to RED/GREEN/REFACTOR)
- Commit signing + verification
- Commit templates for enforcing RED→GREEN→REFACTOR message format
- How `git bisect` interacts with TDD commit sequences

### 5. Enforcement mechanisms
- Pre-commit hooks (run tests on RED commit to verify it fails)
- Pre-push hooks (ratchet check before push)
- GitHub branch protection rules (require status checks, required reviewers)
- CI gates (GitHub Actions, local `act`)
- gitlint / commitlint for message format

### 6. Tooling
- git-branchless: alternative commit graph, virtual branches, `sl` (Sapling)
- Graphite.dev: stacked PRs with auto-rebase
- ghstack: stacked PRs on GitHub without Graphite
- Jujutsu (jj): op log, immutable commits, automatic conflict resolution, anonymous branches
- gitoxide: fast Rust git implementation
- Sapling (Meta's SCM): trunk-based, virtual branches

## Output format

Produce a structured markdown document covering each dimension above. For each strategy: name, how it works in 2-3 sentences, strengths for datum's use case, weaknesses/risks. Be concrete — cite specific git commands or config where relevant. Dense is better than padded.

This output goes directly into an architect agent's context — make it information-dense, not conversational.

- **Epic branches**: `datum/epic-NN-description` off main

- **Parallel act agents**: multiple Claude Code sub-agents work on different TDD lanes simultaneously on the same branch. This causes file-lock collisions (datum#129 — agents using `git checkout` wipe each other's working-tree changes).
- **Squash before first push**: all local commits squash into one before the branch is published.
- **Hard gates**: plan_human_approval, triage_human_approval, merge_human_approval halt the pipeline until a human confirms.
- **Ratchet enforcement**: test count must never go below a floor (currently 829). The gate is checked before merge.
- **Act phase can have 5-15 TDD tasks running in parallel** across units A→F, some serial (A→B→C audio path) and some truly parallel (D/E/F).
- **Problem to solve**: parallel agents on one branch collide. We need an architecture where parallel TDD agents can work without stomping each other, then merge cleanly to the epic branch.

## What to research

Produce findings across these dimensions:

### 1. Branch strategies for parallel work
- Git worktrees (one worktree per parallel agent, merge to epic branch after)
- Feature sub-branches (one branch per TDD task, PR to epic branch)
- Stacked PRs / stacked diffs (Graphite, ghstack, git-branchless)
- Trunk-based with short-lived branches
- What big monorepo shops do (Google, Meta, Stripe)

### 2. Merge strategies
- Squash merge: pros/cons for aggregating multi-commit TDD work
- Rebase merge: preserves RED/GREEN/REFACTOR granularity, rebases onto epic branch
- Merge commit: creates explicit topology showing when parallel lanes merged
- Octopus merge: can merge 3+ branches simultaneously (risky but fast)
- Fast-forward only: strictest, requires linear history

### 3. Conflict resolution patterns for parallel agents
- Worktree isolation (each agent gets own worktree, no shared working tree)
- File-lock protocol (claim files before editing — git-based or external)
- Actor model for git ops (one git-ops coordinator, agents submit diffs)
- Patch-queue model (agents produce patches, coordinator applies serially)
- Pre-merge CI gate per agent lane

### 4. Commit discipline for TDD pipelines
- Conventional commits (feat/fix/test/refactor prefixes)
- Atomic commits (one logical change per commit — maps well to RED/GREEN/REFACTOR)
- Commit signing + verification
- Commit templates for enforcing RED→GREEN→REFACTOR message format
- How `git bisect` interacts with TDD commit sequences

### 5. Enforcement mechanisms
- Pre-commit hooks (run tests on RED commit to verify it fails)
- Pre-push hooks (ratchet check before push)
- GitHub branch protection rules (require status checks, required reviewers)
- CI gates (GitHub Actions, local `act`)
- gitlint / commitlint for message format

### 6. Tooling
- git-branchless: alternative commit graph, virtual branches, `sl` (Sapling)
- Graphite.dev: stacked PRs with auto-rebase
- ghstack: stacked PRs on GitHub without Graphite

## Jujutsu (jj) Technical Reference

### 1. Core Concepts

#### Change ID vs Commit ID

jj uses **two distinct identifiers** for every unit of work:

| Property | Change ID | Commit ID |
|----------|-----------|-----------|
| **Purpose** | Tracks a change as it evolves over time | Identifies a specific immutable snapshot |
| **Format** | 16 random bytes, displayed as 12 letters in **k-z range** (e.g. `qzmzpxyl`) | 20 bytes (Git backend), displayed as 12 hex digits (e.g. `bc915fcd`) |
| **Stability** | **Stable** -- survives amend, rebase, describe | **Changes** on any content/metadata modification |
| **Namespace** | Disjoint from commit IDs (letters k-z only) | Standard hex digits |

The change ID is the key innovation: it gives every unit of work a persistent identity regardless of rewrites. When you `jj describe -m "..."`, the change ID stays the same but the commit ID changes.

#### Anonymous Branches

jj does **not require named branches**. Any commit with no descendants is a "head" tracked by the repo's view. Two commits sharing the same parent naturally form a branch -- no naming ceremony needed.

- jj keeps anonymous branch heads around until explicitly abandoned (unlike Git, which GC's detached commits)
- List all branch tips: `jj log -r 'heads(all())'`
- Creating a branch: just `jj new <parent-change-id>` from a shared ancestor

Log visualization of anonymous branches:
```
@  xrslwzvq  a70d464c  (empty) create hello and goodbye functions
|
| o  yykpmnuq  210283e8  (empty) add better documentation
|/
o  ootnlvpt  b5db7940  only print hello world
```

#### Bookmarks (Named Branches)

Bookmarks are jj's equivalent of Git branches, with a critical behavioral difference: **bookmarks do NOT auto-advance** when you create new commits.

```bash
jj bookmark create trunk              # Create pointing at @
jj bookmark set trunk                 # Move to current @
jj bookmark set trunk -r <rev>        # Move to specific revision
jj bookmark set trunk --allow-backwards  # Allow non-forward moves
jj bookmark delete old-feature        # Delete
jj bookmark list                      # List all
jj bookmark list -a                   # Include remote bookmarks
jj bookmark track main@origin         # Track remote bookmark
```

Remote bookmarks use `@` notation: `trunk@origin`, `main@upstream`.

#### Operation Log

Every repo-mutating command is recorded as an **operation** containing a full snapshot ("view") of all bookmark positions, heads, tags, and working-copy state.

```bash
jj op log                             # Show operation history
jj undo                               # Reverse last operation
jj op restore <op-id>                 # Restore entire repo to a prior state
jj op revert <op-id>                  # Revert a specific non-recent operation
jj --at-op=<op-id> log               # Time-travel: view repo at a past operation
```

Key properties:
- Operations form a DAG (supports concurrent ops on distributed FS)
- `@` = current operation; `@-` = previous operation
- `--at-op` disables auto-snapshotting and resolves `@` to that operation's working-copy commit
- Enables **lock-free concurrency** -- multiple `jj` commands can run simultaneously

#### Conflict Handling

**No jj command ever fails because of a conflict.** Conflicts are stored as first-class data inside commits.

- Rebase continues through conflicts, marking commits as conflicted
- When you resolve a parent conflict, descendants auto-rebase and conflicts may auto-resolve
- Conflict markers use an extended format with snapshots + diffs:

```
<<<<<<<
+++++++
    print("Hello, world!");
    print("Goodbye, world!");
%%%%%%%
     print_hello();
-    print_goodbye();
>>>>>>>
```

`+++++++` = snapshot side, `%%%%%%%` = diff side.

Resolution methods:
```bash
jj resolve                            # Launch external merge tool
jj resolve <path>                     # Resolve specific file
jj resolve --tool=:ours               # Take our side
jj resolve --tool=:theirs             # Take their side
jj resolve --list                     # List conflicted files
```

---

### 2. Key Commands -- Exact Syntax

#### Repository Setup

```bash
jj git init --colocate                # Init in existing git repo (colocated)
jj git clone <url>                    # Clone from git remote
jj config set --user user.name "Name"
jj config set --user user.email "email@example.com"
```

#### Working with Changes

```bash
jj new                                # Create empty change on top of @
jj new <rev>                          # Create change with specific parent
jj new -m "message"                   # Create with description
jj new -B @                           # Create change BEFORE current (insert)
jj describe -m "message"              # Set/update description of @
jj commit -m "message"                # Shortcut: describe @ + jj new
jj edit <change-id>                   # Switch working copy to edit a specific change
jj abandon                            # Discard current change, rebase descendants onto parent
```

#### Moving Changes Between Commits

```bash
jj squash                             # Move all @ changes into parent (@-)
jj squash src/main.rs                 # Squash only specific files
jj squash -i                          # Interactive TUI selection
jj squash --into <dest>               # Squash @ into a specific (non-parent) commit
jj squash -r <src> --into <dest>      # Squash one commit into another
jj split                              # Split @ into two commits
jj split -i                           # Interactive split
jj absorb                             # Auto-distribute changes to appropriate ancestor commits
```

#### Rebasing

```bash
jj rebase -d <dest>                   # Rebase @ and descendants onto <dest>
jj rebase -r <rev> -d <dest>          # Rebase specific revision
jj parallelize <revset>               # Convert linear stack to parallel siblings
```

Automatic rebasing: when you rewrite any commit, **all descendants auto-rebase**. No manual intervention. Change IDs remain stable; commit IDs update.

#### Navigation

```bash
jj prev                               # Move to parent commit (creates new change)
jj next                               # Move to child commit (creates new change)
jj prev --edit                         # Edit parent directly (no new change)
jj next --edit                         # Edit child directly
```

#### Viewing

```bash
jj status                             # (alias: jj st) Show working copy state
jj log                                # Show commit graph
jj log -r <revset>                    # Filter by revset
jj log -n 5                           # Limit output
jj diff                               # Show changes in @
jj diff -r <rev>                      # Diff a specific revision
jj diff --from <a> --to <b>           # Compare two revisions
jj diff -s                            # Summary only
jj evolog                             # Evolution log: history of a change's rewrites
jj interdiff --from <a> --to <b>      # Compare two versions of same change
```

#### Remote Operations

```bash
jj git fetch                           # Fetch from origin
jj git fetch --all-remotes             # Fetch from all remotes
jj git push                            # Push all tracked bookmarks
jj git push --bookmark <name>          # Push specific bookmark
jj git push --bookmark <name> --allow-new  # First push of a new bookmark
jj git push -c @                       # Auto-create bookmark from change ID and push
jj git push -n                         # Dry run
```

```bash

## Sapling (sl) Version Control -- Technical Reference

### Part 1: Parallel Development Workflow

#### The Core Mental Model Shift

**Git**: Your repository is defined by branch names. You must be on a named branch to do work. Parallel work = multiple named branches.

**Sapling**: Branch names (called "bookmarks") are completely optional. **The stack is the branch.** You create commits that fork off main and they are visible in your smartlog by hash. No label needed. Parallel work = multiple independent stacks, all visible at a glance.

Key differences:
- **No staging area** -- `sl commit` takes working directory changes directly (use `-i` for interactive selection)
- **No branch creation ceremony** -- just commit; it forks automatically if you're not at the tip
- **Commits are never truly deleted** -- they are hidden/unhidden (`sl hide` / `sl unhide`)
- **Mutation history is tracked** -- amend, rebase, fold, split all record predecessors, enabling automatic restacking across machines
- **Each command does one thing** -- `pull` only fetches, `goto` only moves, `checkout` is not overloaded like git's

#### Creating Parallel Stacks

```bash
# Start first piece of work (no branch name needed)
sl goto main
echo "feature A" > a.txt && sl add a.txt
sl commit -m "feature A: foundation"
echo "more A" >> a.txt
sl commit -m "feature A: polish"

# Start second piece of work -- just go back to main
sl goto main
echo "feature B" > b.txt && sl add b.txt
sl commit -m "feature B: implementation"

# Now 'sl' (smartlog) shows TWO independent stacks
```

Smartlog output for parallel stacks:

```
  o  abc123  2 min ago  you
  │  feature A: polish
  │
  o  def456  3 min ago  you
╭─╯  feature A: foundation
│
│ o  789abc  1 min ago  you
├─╯  feature B: implementation
│
o  000000  10 min ago  remote/main
```

Each stack is visually distinct. No branch names cluttering the view.

#### Stack Navigation

```bash
sl prev          # move down one commit in current stack
sl next          # move up one commit in current stack
sl top           # jump to tip of current stack
sl bottom        # jump to base of current stack (first draft commit)
sl next 2        # move up two commits
sl goto HASH     # jump to any commit by hash
```

No need to remember branch names or type long hashes -- just navigate spatially.

#### Editing Commits Mid-Stack

```bash
# Edit a commit that's NOT at the top
sl goto def456                  # go to the commit you want to edit
# ... make changes ...
sl amend                        # amend that commit in place
# Sapling AUTOMATICALLY rebases all commits above it
```

This is the killer feature vs `git rebase -i`. No interactive editor, no conflict-prone multi-step rebase. Just goto, edit, amend, done. Downstream commits restack automatically.

#### Advanced Stack Manipulation

```bash
# Absorb: auto-route uncommitted changes to the right commit in the stack
sl absorb              # analyzes changed lines, matches to originating commit

# Amend to specific commit (when absorb can't determine target)
sl amend --to HASH     # explicitly target a specific commit

# Fold: merge multiple commits into one
sl fold --from HASH    # fold from HASH down to current commit
sl fold --exact HASH1 HASH2  # fold specific commits

# Split: break one commit into multiple
sl split               # interactive editor to divide changes

# Restack: fix up the stack after manual operations
sl restack
```

#### Submitting Stacks for Review

```bash
# Submit entire stack as one-PR-per-commit
sl pr submit           # creates/updates GitHub PRs for each commit in stack

# Check PR status in smartlog
sl ssl                 # "super smartlog" -- shows PR numbers, CI status, review state
```

#### Parallel Worktree Pattern (from ezyang's blog)

For truly parallel work (e.g., multiple agents or workflows simultaneously):

```bash
# Critical aliases for parallel coordination
[alias]
follow = goto last(successors(.))    # chase a commit after it's been amended
adopt = rebase -s 'children(parents(.)) - .' -d .  # rebase orphaned children onto current
```

**`sl follow` pattern**: When someone amends a parent commit and it restacks, your worktree is on the stale version. Run `sl follow` to jump to the successor commit, preserving uncommitted changes.

**`sl adopt` pattern**: After inserting a new commit mid-stack, run `sl adopt` to rebase the old children onto your new commit, preventing forks.

Parallel agent workflow:
1. Agent A amends commit at stack base --> auto-restacks everything above
2. Agent B (on a mid-stack commit) runs `sl follow` to catch up to the new version
3. Agent B commits new work, then `sl adopt` to rebase Agent C's commits on top
4. Agent C runs `sl follow` to chase the full successor chain

#### Undo/Recovery (Better Than Git)

```bash
sl undo              # undo last operation (any operation)
sl redo              # redo it
sl uncommit          # undo a commit, keep changes in working directory
sl unamend           # undo an amend
sl hide HASH         # hide a commit (not delete -- recoverable)
sl unhide HASH       # bring it back
sl undo -i           # INTERACTIVE: browse historical smartlog snapshots, pick state to restore
```

---

### Part 2: Smartlog and Virtual Filesystem

#### Smartlog (`sl` or `sl smartlog`)

The single most important command. Shows your entire local state in one view.

**What it displays:**
- All your unpushed/draft commits
- Location of `remote/main` and other configured bookmarks
- Graph relationships (parent/child)
- Your current position (where your working directory is)
- Obsolete commits (landed, amended, rebased away)

**Graph symbols:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `o` | Regular draft commit |
| `@` | Your current working directory position |
| `x` | Obsolete commit (landed/amended/rebased) |
| `│` | Ancestry line |
| `╭─╯` | Branch/fork connection |
| `~` | Elided (hidden) commits to reduce noise |
| `---` (dashed) | Main branch (hides thousands of irrelevant commits) |

**Example smartlog with parallel stacks and landed work:**

```
  o  abc123  10 min ago  you
  │  Wire up the new endpoint
  │
  @  def456  10 min ago  you
  │  Add request validation
  │
  o  789abc  10 min ago  you
╭─╯  Define the schema
│
│ x  old111  yesterday  you  (Landed as aaa222)
├─╯  Fix the login bug
│
o  000000  1 hour ago  remote/main
```

Reading this:
- You have one active stack of 3 commits (schema -> validation -> endpoint)
- Your working directory (`@`) is on "Add request validation"
- "Fix the login bug" landed (merged to main) -- shown as `x` with the landed hash
- `remote/main` is the public baseline

The **kink** (`╭─╯`) marks the public/draft boundary -- everything above is your unpublished work.

#### Smartlog Variants

```bash
sl                  # basic smartlog (default, most common)
sl smartlog         # same as above, explicit

sl ssl              # "super smartlog" -- fetches GitHub data
                    # shows PR numbers, CI status, review comments

sl web              # launches Interactive Smartlog (ISL) in browser
                    # auto-refreshing, drag-and-drop rebasing
```

#### Interactive Smartlog (ISL)

Launched via `sl web`. A browser-based GUI that provides:

- **Visual commit tree** with "You are here" indicator
- **Drag-and-drop rebasing** -- literally drag a commit to rebase it (blocked when uncommitted changes exist)
- **Inline commit/amend** -- buttons to create or amend commits with sidebar for messages
- **Change comparison views**:
  - Uncommitted Changes (`Cmd+'`)
  - Head Changes (`Cmd+Shift+'`)
  - Stack Changes (all changes back to main)
  - Committed Changes (single commit)
- **PR integration** -- shows PR status badges, CI builds, comment counts
- **Conflict resolution** -- marks unresolved files with checkboxes
- **Command queueing** -- operations queue; if one fails, subsequent ones auto-cancel

Remote access:
```bash
# On remote machine
sl isl --no-open -p 5000

# Option 1: Direct (if port open)
# Open http://remote-host:5000/?token=...

# Option 2: SSH tunnel
ssh -L 4000:localhost:5000 -N user@remote-host
# Open http://localhost:4000/?token=...
```

#### Virtual Filesystem (EdenFS)

EdenFS is Sapling's virtual filesystem layer for massive repos. Key facts:

- **Not yet publicly supported** -- used in production at Meta, not released for external use
- Makes the entire repo appear checked out while only materializing files on access
- First file access requires a network request; subsequent accesses are cached
- Clones and checkouts become near-instant regardless of repo size
- Complements **sparse profiles** (shareable `.sparse` files checked into the repo that define which subset of the monorepo a developer needs)

#### Scalability Stack (What Makes It Work at Scale)

| Layer | Problem | Solution |
|-------|---------|----------|
| History | Millions of commits | **Segmented Changelog** -- lazy-loads commits on demand; clone downloads almost nothing |
| File content | Millions of files | **On-demand fetching** -- trees and blobs fetched as needed |
| Working copy | Can't checkout millions of files | **EdenFS** (virtual FS) or **sparse profiles** |
| Status | `sl status` on huge repos | **Watchman** integration -- filesystem monitor, no full scan |
| Graph queries | Common ancestor in huge DAGs | O(number-of-merges) algorithm via segmented changelog |
| Per-file history | `sl log FILE` in old repos | Dedicated per-file history graph on server -- sub-second regardless of age |

#### Commit Cloud (Not Yet Public)

All commits in your org are uploaded as they're made. Sharing code = send a hash:
```bash
# Colleague sends you hash abc123
sl goto abc123    # just works -- commit cloud fetches it
```

No push/pull dance, no branch naming, no PR needed for WIP sharing.

#### Practitioner Tips

1. **Stop thinking in branches.** Think in stacks. Your smartlog IS your branch manager.
2. **`sl` is your `git status` + `git log` + `git branch` combined.** Run it constantly.
3. **Amend freely.** Mutation tracking means restacking is automatic and safe. In git, amending mid-stack is terrifying; in Sapling, it's the normal workflow.
4. **Use `sl absorb` over manual `goto` + `amend`** when editing lines that originated in specific stack commits -- it auto-routes changes.
5. **`sl undo -i`** is the panic button -- browse historical snapshots of your repo state and jump back to any point.
6. **`sl pr submit` over manual PR creation** -- it manages the one-PR-per-commit model automatically.
7. **For parallel agents/worktrees**, define `follow` and `adopt` aliases (see above) -- they're essential for keeping multiple workers synchronized on a shared stack.
8. **ISL (`sl web`) for complex operations** -- drag-and-drop rebase is faster and less error-prone than CLI for rearranging stacks.
9. **Sapling is optimized for single-master, rebase-over-merge, always-online workflows.** It works with GitHub repos via `sl clone --git`, but its sweet spot is that corporate monorepo pattern.
10. **No staging area by design.** Use `sl commit -i` or `sl amend -i` for interactive hunk selection when you need partial commits.

| Operation | Git | Sapling |
|-----------|-----|---------|
| View state | `git status` + `git log --graph` + `git branch` | `sl` |
| Create branch | `git checkout -b name` | Just commit (no name needed) |
| Switch branch | `git checkout name` | `sl goto HASH` |
| Navigate stack | `git log`, copy hash, `git checkout` | `sl prev` / `sl next` / `sl top` / `sl bottom` |
| Edit mid-stack commit | `git rebase -i` (complex) | `sl goto HASH` + edit + `sl amend` (auto-restacks) |
| Auto-route fixes to right commit | N/A | `sl absorb` |
| Merge commits | `git rebase -i` + squash | `sl fold` |
| Split commit | `git rebase -i` + edit (manual) | `sl split` (interactive) |
| Undo anything | `git reflog` + `git reset` (risky) | `sl undo` / `sl undo -i` (safe, visual) |

| Visual UI | GitKraken / lazygit (third-party) | `sl web` (built-in ISL) |

## `git merge --squash` -- Deep Technical Internals

### 1. What `git merge --squash` Does at the Plumbing Level

At the source code level (`builtin/merge.c`), `git merge --squash` runs the **exact same three-way merge algorithm** as a regular merge (using the `ort` strategy by default, previously `recursive`). The merge strategies (`ort`, `recursive`, `resolve`, `octopus`, `subtree`) execute identically regardless of `--squash`. The divergence happens entirely in the **post-merge bookkeeping**.

**Exact sequence of operations:**

1. **Find the merge base** -- Git computes the common ancestor of HEAD and the target branch using `merge-base`. For `ort`/`recursive`, this handles criss-cross merges via recursive ancestor consolidation.

2. **Perform three-way merge** -- The merge strategy performs a three-way merge between:
   - Stage 1: the common ancestor (merge base)
   - Stage 2: the current HEAD
   - Stage 3: the incoming branch tip
   
   This updates the **index** (staging area) and the **working tree** identically to a normal merge. Cleanly merged paths go to stage 0 in the index. Conflicting paths populate stages 1/2/3 (viewable via `git ls-files -u`).

3. **Post-merge divergence** -- Here is where `--squash` departs. In a regular merge, the `finish()` function:
   - Writes `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_HEAD` (pointing to the merged branch tip)
   - Writes `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_MODE`
   - Writes `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_MSG` (the merge commit message template)
   - Updates the HEAD ref to point to the new merge commit
   - Creates the merge commit with **two parent pointers**

   With `--squash`, the `finish()` function instead:
   - Calls `squash_message()` which writes `$GIT_DIR/SQUASH_MSG` (NOT `MERGE_MSG`)
   - **Does NOT** write `MERGE_HEAD`
   - **Does NOT** write `MERGE_MODE`
   - **Does NOT** update HEAD
   - **Does NOT** create any commit
   - Prints: `Squash commit -- not updating HEAD`

4. **Post-merge hook** -- The hook **always runs**, but receives argument `"1"` for squash (vs `"0"` for normal merge):
   ```c
   run_hooks_l(the_repository, "post-merge", squash ? "1" : "0", NULL);
   ```

5. **User commits manually** -- The user runs `git commit`, which creates a commit with a **single parent** (current HEAD). Git uses `SQUASH_MSG` as the default commit message template.

**Key source code references** (from `git/builtin/merge.c`):
- Line 72: `static int squash;` -- global flag
- Lines 297-323: `squash_message()` -- walks the revision list of the incoming branch, pretty-prints each commit message, writes to `SQUASH_MSG`
- Lines 327-357: `finish()` -- the conditional block that skips `refs_update_ref()` for HEAD when `squash` is true
- Line 320: `write_file_buf(git_path_squash_msg(the_repository), out.buf, out.len);`

### 2. Effect on the Commit DAG (Parent Pointers)

**Regular merge commit:**
```
      A---B---C  (feature)
     /         \
D---E---F---G---M  (main)
```
Commit `M` has **two parents**: `G` (first parent, from main) and `C` (second parent, from feature). You can verify with:
```bash
git cat-file -p M
# tree <hash>
# parent <hash-of-G>
# parent <hash-of-C>
# author ...
```

**Squash merge commit:**
```
      A---B---C  (feature)
     /
D---E---F---G---S  (main)
```
Commit `S` has **one parent**: `G`. There is **no reference** to `C` or any commit on the feature branch. The tree object of `S` is content-identical to what `M`'s tree would have been, but the ancestry link is severed.
```bash
git cat-file -p S
# tree <hash>       (same tree hash as M would have)
# parent <hash-of-G> (ONLY one parent)
# author ...
```

**Why only one parent:** Because `--squash` does not write `MERGE_HEAD`, the subsequent `git commit` has no way to know about the second parent. When `git commit` creates a commit object, it reads `MERGE_HEAD` to determine if additional parents should be recorded. Since `MERGE_HEAD` does not exist after `--squash`, the commit is created as a normal single-parent commit. The tree snapshot is identical -- only the parent pointers differ.

### 3. Index and Working Tree During --squash

The index and working tree are updated **identically** to a regular merge:

**Clean merge (no conflicts):**
- All merged paths are written to **stage 0** in the index (fully resolved)
- Working tree files contain the merged content
- State is ready for `git commit`

**Merge with conflicts:**
- Conflicting paths have entries at **stages 1, 2, and 3** in the index:
  - Stage 1: common ancestor version
  - Stage 2: HEAD (ours) version
  - Stage 3: incoming (theirs) version
- Working tree files contain conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`)
- You can inspect with `git ls-files -u`
- You resolve, `git add`, then `git commit`

**What differs from regular merge:** The only difference is that after `--squash` with conflicts, `MERGE_HEAD` does not exist. This means `git merge --abort` will not work the same way (since `git merge --abort` is equivalent to `git reset --merge` when `MERGE_HEAD` is present). To abort a squash merge, you use `git reset --merge` directly.

### 4. Merge Info Recording

| File | Regular Merge | `--squash` |
|------|--------------|------------|
| `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_HEAD` | Written (points to merged branch tip) | **NOT written** |
| `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_MODE` | Written | **NOT written** |
| `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_MSG` | Written (template for merge commit message) | **NOT written** |
| `$GIT_DIR/SQUASH_MSG` | NOT written | **Written** (contains all squashed commit messages) |
| `$GIT_DIR/AUTO_MERGE` | Written by `ort` strategy on conflict | Written by `ort` strategy on conflict |

The `SQUASH_MSG` file is generated by the `squash_message()` function, which:
1. Initializes a revision walker
2. Marks the current HEAD as `UNINTERESTING`
3. Adds all remote head commits as pending objects
4. Walks the revisions (all commits reachable from the branch tip but not from HEAD)
5. Pretty-prints each commit's OID and message
6. Writes the concatenated result to `SQUASH_MSG`

When you subsequently run `git commit`, Git picks up `SQUASH_MSG` as the default message template (you can edit it in your editor). This is why the default squash commit message contains all the individual commit messages from the branch.

### 5. GitHub's "Squash and Merge" Button vs Manual `git merge --squash`

**GitHub's API endpoint:**
```
PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{pull_number}/merge
```
With body parameter `"merge_method": "squash"`.

**Key behavioral differences:**

| Aspect | Manual `git merge --squash` | GitHub "Squash and Merge" |
|--------|---------------------------|--------------------------|
| Commit creation | Two-step: merge then commit | Atomic single operation |
| Fast-forward | Does NOT use fast-forward | Uses the **fast-forward option** per GitHub docs |
| Commit message | `SQUASH_MSG` (all commit messages concatenated) | Configurable: PR title only, PR title + commit list, PR title + description, or single commit's message |
| Commit author | Whoever runs `git commit` | The PR author (GitHub preserves authorship) |
| Server-side | N/A | GitHub creates a new commit object server-side, computes the tree, sets a single parent pointing to the base branch tip |
| API response | N/A | Returns `{"sha": "...", "merged": true, "message": "..."}` |
| `commit_title` | Set by user at commit time | API parameter or UI field |
| `sha` verification | N/A | API supports `sha` param to ensure HEAD hasn't moved (optimistic concurrency) |

**GitHub's commit message defaults** (configurable per-repository):
- 1 commit in PR: uses the commit's title and message
- 2+ commits: uses the PR title as the commit title, with a list of all commits in the body
- Alternative settings: PR title only, PR title + commit details, PR title + description

**GitHub internally** does not run `git merge --squash`. It computes the merge result server-side (likely using `libgit2` or their own merge infrastructure), generates a single commit object with one parent pointing to the base branch tip, and fast-forwards the base branch ref to that new commit.

### 6. Implications for `git bisect`

**Advantages of squash-merged history for bisect:**

- **Linear history** means bisect performs a clean binary search. With N commits, bisect finds the culprit in approximately log2(N) steps.
- **No broken intermediate commits.** Feature branches often contain commits that don't compile, fail tests, or represent partial work. Bisect landing on these is a dead end. Squash merges guarantee each commit on main is a complete, testable unit.
- **No `--first-parent` needed.** With merge commits, bisect can follow the wrong branch into feature branch history. The `--first-parent` flag exists specifically to work around this:
  ```bash
  git bisect start --first-parent
  ```
  With squash merges, this flag is unnecessary -- there is only one parent per commit.

**Disadvantages:**

- **Coarse granularity.** Each squash commit can represent hundreds of lines across dozens of files. When bisect identifies a squash commit as the culprit, you still need to manually narrow down which change within that commit caused the regression. With preserved merge history, bisect could have drilled into the feature branch commits.
- **Cannot revert surgically.** With merge commits, you can `git revert -m 1 <merge-commit>` to undo an entire feature. With squash commits, `git revert <squash-commit>` works but produces a large inverse diff that may conflict with subsequent squash commits.

**Performance comparison:**

```
# Merge-commit history (100 merges, avg 10 commits each = 1000 total commits)
# bisect without --first-parent: ~10 steps, but may land on broken commits
# bisect with --first-parent: ~7 steps, only tests merge commits

# Squash-merged history (100 squash commits)
# bisect: ~7 steps, each commit is guaranteed testable
# But each "step" tests a larger diff
```

**The `--first-parent` flag in detail:** Follows only the first parent at merge commits. The merge commit itself is identified as the introduction point, and ancestors in the merged branch are ignored. This prevents false positives from non-buildable commits in merged branches. Effectively, `--first-parent` on merge-commit history approximates what squash-merged history gives you natively.

### 7. Commit Message Best Practices

Based on production experience (notably DNSimple's two-year squash-merge study):

1. **Write a fresh, descriptive message.** Do not accept the default concatenated `SQUASH_MSG` as-is. Write a message that explains the *why*, not just the *what*.

2. **Reference the PR.** Always include a link or reference to the original pull request (e.g., `(#123)`). The PR is the source of truth -- it contains the full conversation, individual commits, and reviewer feedback.

3. **Use conventional commit format if your project uses it:**
   ```
   feat(auth): add OAuth2 PKCE flow for mobile clients (#123)
   
   Implements RFC 7636 code challenge for the mobile app login flow.
   Replaces the implicit grant which was deprecated by the OAuth 2.1 draft.
   ```

4. **GitHub's configurable defaults** (set at the repository level):
   - PR title only
   - PR title + commit details
   - PR title + PR description
   - Single commit title + message (when PR has 1 commit)

5. **Credit contributors** if the squash aggregates work from multiple authors.

6. **Do not include** "fix typo", "fix CI", "address review comments" noise. The squash commit message should be the polished final version.

### 8. Problems When Re-Merging a Squash-Merged Branch

This is the most significant footgun of squash merges.

**The problem:**
```
      A---B---C  (feature-1, squash-merged to main as S)
     /         \
D---E-----------S  (main, after squash merge)
     \
      A---B---C---X---Y  (feature-2, branched from feature-1)
```

When you try to merge `feature-2` into `main`:

```bash
git merge-base main feature-2
# Returns commit E  (NOT commit C or S)
```

Git computes the merge base as commit `E` -- the original fork point. Because the squash commit `S` has no parent pointer to `C`, Git does not know that commits `A`, `B`, `C` are already incorporated into `main`. The three-way merge therefore:

1. Computes diff from `E` to `S` (main's changes, including the squashed A+B+C content)
2. Computes diff from `E` to `Y` (feature-2's changes, which ALSO include A+B+C content)
3. Finds **duplicate changes** in both diffs and reports conflicts

**With a regular merge commit,** the merge base would advance to `C` (because `C` is reachable from both `M` and `feature-2`), and the three-way merge would correctly see only `X` and `Y` as new changes.

**Concrete demonstration:**
```bash
# Setup
git init && echo "base" > file.txt && git add . && git commit -m "init"
git checkout -b feature-1
echo "feature work" >> file.txt && git commit -am "A"
echo "more work" >> file.txt && git commit -am "B"

# Squash merge feature-1 into main
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature-1
git commit -m "squash feature-1"

# Branch feature-2 from feature-1
git checkout feature-1
git checkout -b feature-2
echo "new work" >> file.txt && git commit -am "X"

# Try to merge feature-2 into main -- CONFLICTS
git checkout main
git merge feature-2
# CONFLICT: Git sees duplicate changes from A and B
```

**Workarounds:**

1. **Delete the branch after squash merge.** Never continue work on a squash-merged branch. Create a new branch from `main` if you need to continue.
2. **Use `git rebase main` on the dependent branch** after the squash merge, which replays only the new commits onto the updated main.
3. **Use `git reset --soft main`** on the dependent branch to collapse everything into a single diff against the current main, then re-commit.
4. **Do not squash merge** when branches have descendants that will be merged later. Use regular merge commits for long-lived branches with child branches.

**Relevant commands to diagnose:**
```bash
# Check the merge base between two branches
git merge-base main feature-2

# See the commit graph to understand parent relationships
git log --oneline --graph --all

# Inspect a commit's parents
git cat-file -p <commit-sha>

# List conflicting files with their index stages
git ls-files -u
```

## Sapling (sl) Version Control -- Technical Reference

### Part 1: Parallel Development Workflow

#### The Core Mental Model Shift

**Git**: Your repository is defined by branch names. You must be on a named branch to do work. Parallel work = multiple named branches.

**Sapling**: Branch names (called "bookmarks") are completely optional. **The stack is the branch.** You create commits that fork off main and they are visible in your smartlog by hash. No label needed. Parallel work = multiple independent stacks, all visible at a glance.

Key differences:
- **No staging area** -- `sl commit` takes working directory changes directly (use `-i` for interactive selection)
- **No branch creation ceremony** -- just commit; it forks automatically if you're not at the tip
- **Commits are never truly deleted** -- they are hidden/unhidden (`sl hide` / `sl unhide`)
- **Mutation history is tracked** -- amend, rebase, fold, split all record predecessors, enabling automatic restacking across machines
- **Each command does one thing** -- `pull` only fetches, `goto` only moves, `checkout` is not overloaded like git's

#### Creating Parallel Stacks

```bash
# Start first piece of work (no branch name needed)
sl goto main
echo "feature A" > a.txt && sl add a.txt
sl commit -m "feature A: foundation"
echo "more A" >> a.txt
sl commit -m "feature A: polish"

# Start second piece of work -- just go back to main
sl goto main
echo "feature B" > b.txt && sl add b.txt
sl commit -m "feature B: implementation"

# Now 'sl' (smartlog) shows TWO independent stacks
```

Smartlog output for parallel stacks:

```
  o  abc123  2 min ago  you
  │  feature A: polish
  │
  o  def456  3 min ago  you
╭─╯  feature A: foundation
│
│ o  789abc  1 min ago  you
├─╯  feature B: implementation
│
o  000000  10 min ago  remote/main
```

Each stack is visually distinct. No branch names cluttering the view.

#### Stack Navigation

```bash
sl prev          # move down one commit in current stack
sl next          # move up one commit in current stack
sl top           # jump to tip of current stack
sl bottom        # jump to base of current stack (first draft commit)
sl next 2        # move up two commits
sl goto HASH     # jump to any commit by hash
```

No need to remember branch names or type long hashes -- just navigate spatially.

#### Editing Commits Mid-Stack

```bash
# Edit a commit that's NOT at the top
sl goto def456                  # go to the commit you want to edit
# ... make changes ...
sl amend                        # amend that commit in place
# Sapling AUTOMATICALLY rebases all commits above it
```

This is the killer feature vs `git rebase -i`. No interactive editor, no conflict-prone multi-step rebase. Just goto, edit, amend, done. Downstream commits restack automatically.

#### Advanced Stack Manipulation

```bash
# Absorb: auto-route uncommitted changes to the right commit in the stack
sl absorb              # analyzes changed lines, matches to originating commit

# Amend to specific commit (when absorb can't determine target)
sl amend --to HASH     # explicitly target a specific commit

# Fold: merge multiple commits into one
sl fold --from HASH    # fold from HASH down to current commit
sl fold --exact HASH1 HASH2  # fold specific commits

# Split: break one commit into multiple
sl split               # interactive editor to divide changes

# Restack: fix up the stack after manual operations
sl restack
```

#### Submitting Stacks for Review

```bash
# Submit entire stack as one-PR-per-commit
sl pr submit           # creates/updates GitHub PRs for each commit in stack

# Check PR status in smartlog
sl ssl                 # "super smartlog" -- shows PR numbers, CI status, review state
```

#### Parallel Worktree Pattern (from ezyang's blog)

For truly parallel work (e.g., multiple agents or workflows simultaneously):

```bash
# Critical aliases for parallel coordination
[alias]
follow = goto last(successors(.))    # chase a commit after it's been amended
adopt = rebase -s 'children(parents(.)) - .' -d .  # rebase orphaned children onto current
```

**`sl follow` pattern**: When someone amends a parent commit and it restacks, your worktree is on the stale version. Run `sl follow` to jump to the successor commit, preserving uncommitted changes.

**`sl adopt` pattern**: After inserting a new commit mid-stack, run `sl adopt` to rebase the old children onto your new commit, preventing forks.

Parallel agent workflow:
1. Agent A amends commit at stack base --> auto-restacks everything above
2. Agent B (on a mid-stack commit) runs `sl follow` to catch up to the new version
3. Agent B commits new work, then `sl adopt` to rebase Agent C's commits on top
4. Agent C runs `sl follow` to chase the full successor chain

#### Undo/Recovery (Better Than Git)

```bash
sl undo              # undo last operation (any operation)
sl redo              # redo it
sl uncommit          # undo a commit, keep changes in working directory
sl unamend           # undo an amend
sl hide HASH         # hide a commit (not delete -- recoverable)
sl unhide HASH       # bring it back
sl undo -i           # INTERACTIVE: browse historical smartlog snapshots, pick state to restore
```

---

### Part 2: Smartlog and Virtual Filesystem

#### Smartlog (`sl` or `sl smartlog`)

The single most important command. Shows your entire local state in one view.

**What it displays:**
- All your unpushed/draft commits
- Location of `remote/main` and other configured bookmarks
- Graph relationships (parent/child)
- Your current position (where your working directory is)
- Obsolete commits (landed, amended, rebased away)

**Graph symbols:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `o` | Regular draft commit |
| `@` | Your current working directory position |
| `x` | Obsolete commit (landed/amended/rebased) |
| `│` | Ancestry line |
| `╭─╯` | Branch/fork connection |
| `~` | Elided (hidden) commits to reduce noise |
| `---` (dashed) | Main branch (hides thousands of irrelevant commits) |

**Example smartlog with parallel stacks and landed work:**

```
  o  abc123  10 min ago  you
  │  Wire up the new endpoint
  │
  @  def456  10 min ago  you
  │  Add request validation
  │
  o  789abc  10 min ago  you
╭─╯  Define the schema
│
│ x  old111  yesterday  you  (Landed as aaa222)
├─╯  Fix the login bug
│
o  000000  1 hour ago  remote/main
```

Reading this:
- You have one active stack of 3 commits (schema -> validation -> endpoint)
- Your working directory (`@`) is on "Add request validation"
- "Fix the login bug" landed (merged to main) -- shown as `x` with the landed hash
- `remote/main` is the public baseline

The **kink** (`╭─╯`) marks the public/draft boundary -- everything above is your unpublished work.

#### Smartlog Variants

```bash
sl                  # basic smartlog (default, most common)
sl smartlog         # same as above, explicit

sl ssl              # "super smartlog" -- fetches GitHub data
                    # shows PR numbers, CI status, review comments

sl web              # launches Interactive Smartlog (ISL) in browser
                    # auto-refreshing, drag-and-drop rebasing
```

#### Interactive Smartlog (ISL)

Launched via `sl web`. A browser-based GUI that provides:

- **Visual commit tree** with "You are here" indicator
- **Drag-and-drop rebasing** -- literally drag a commit to rebase it (blocked when uncommitted changes exist)
- **Inline commit/amend** -- buttons to create or amend commits with sidebar for messages
- **Change comparison views**:
  - Uncommitted Changes (`Cmd+'`)
  - Head Changes (`Cmd+Shift+'`)
  - Stack Changes (all changes back to main)
  - Committed Changes (single commit)
- **PR integration** -- shows PR status badges, CI builds, comment counts
- **Conflict resolution** -- marks unresolved files with checkboxes
- **Command queueing** -- operations queue; if one fails, subsequent ones auto-cancel

Remote access:
```bash
# On remote machine
sl isl --no-open -p 5000

# Option 1: Direct (if port open)
# Open http://remote-host:5000/?token=...

# Option 2: SSH tunnel
ssh -L 4000:localhost:5000 -N user@remote-host
# Open http://localhost:4000/?token=...
```

#### Virtual Filesystem (EdenFS)

EdenFS is Sapling's virtual filesystem layer for massive repos. Key facts:

- **Not yet publicly supported** -- used in production at Meta, not released for external use
- Makes the entire repo appear checked out while only materializing files on access
- First file access requires a network request; subsequent accesses are cached
- Clones and checkouts become near-instant regardless of repo size
- Complements **sparse profiles** (shareable `.sparse` files checked into the repo that define which subset of the monorepo a developer needs)

#### Scalability Stack (What Makes It Work at Scale)

| Layer | Problem | Solution |
|-------|---------|----------|
| History | Millions of commits | **Segmented Changelog** -- lazy-loads commits on demand; clone downloads almost nothing |
| File content | Millions of files | **On-demand fetching** -- trees and blobs fetched as needed |
| Working copy | Can't checkout millions of files | **EdenFS** (virtual FS) or **sparse profiles** |
| Status | `sl status` on huge repos | **Watchman** integration -- filesystem monitor, no full scan |
| Graph queries | Common ancestor in huge DAGs | O(number-of-merges) algorithm via segmented changelog |
| Per-file history | `sl log FILE` in old repos | Dedicated per-file history graph on server -- sub-second regardless of age |

#### Commit Cloud (Not Yet Public)

All commits in your org are uploaded as they're made. Sharing code = send a hash:
```bash
# Colleague sends you hash abc123
sl goto abc123    # just works -- commit cloud fetches it
```

No push/pull dance, no branch naming, no PR needed for WIP sharing.

#### Practitioner Tips

1. **Stop thinking in branches.** Think in stacks. Your smartlog IS your branch manager.
2. **`sl` is your `git status` + `git log` + `git branch` combined.** Run it constantly.
3. **Amend freely.** Mutation tracking means restacking is automatic and safe. In git, amending mid-stack is terrifying; in Sapling, it's the normal workflow.
4. **Use `sl absorb` over manual `goto` + `amend`** when editing lines that originated in specific stack commits -- it auto-routes changes.
5. **`sl undo -i`** is the panic button -- browse historical snapshots of your repo state and jump back to any point.
6. **`sl pr submit` over manual PR creation** -- it manages the one-PR-per-commit model automatically.
7. **For parallel agents/worktrees**, define `follow` and `adopt` aliases (see above) -- they're essential for keeping multiple workers synchronized on a shared stack.
8. **ISL (`sl web`) for complex operations** -- drag-and-drop rebase is faster and less error-prone than CLI for rearranging stacks.
9. **Sapling is optimized for single-master, rebase-over-merge, always-online workflows.** It works with GitHub repos via `sl clone --git`, but its sweet spot is that corporate monorepo pattern.
10. **No staging area by design.** Use `sl commit -i` or `sl amend -i` for interactive hunk selection when you need partial commits.

---

### Command Cheat Sheet: Sapling vs Git

| Operation | Git | Sapling |
|-----------|-----|---------|
| View state | `git status` + `git log --graph` + `git branch` | `sl` |
| Create branch | `git checkout -b name` | Just commit (no name needed) |
| Switch branch | `git checkout name` | `sl goto HASH` |
| Navigate stack | `git log`, copy hash, `git checkout` | `sl prev` / `sl next` / `sl top` / `sl bottom` |
| Edit mid-stack commit | `git rebase -i` (complex) | `sl goto HASH` + edit + `sl amend` (auto-restacks) |
| Auto-route fixes to right commit | N/A | `sl absorb` |
| Merge commits | `git rebase -i` + squash | `sl fold` |
| Split commit | `git rebase -i` + edit (manual) | `sl split` (interactive) |
| Undo anything | `git reflog` + `git reset` (risky) | `sl undo` / `sl undo -i` (safe, visual) |
| Delete branch | `git branch -D name` | `sl hide HASH` (recoverable) |
| Submit for review | manual PR creation | `sl pr submit` (one PR per commit) |
| PR status | `gh pr status` | `sl ssl` (inline in smartlog) |
| Visual UI | GitKraken / lazygit (third-party) | `sl web` (built-in ISL) |
